summary.text: 七 is the numeral character for “seven.” Crossed forms are documented writing the numeral from oracle-bone writing onward, while a competing proposal treats the graph as an earlier sign for cutting that was later borrowed for seven.

formation.text: The formation is disputed. One analysis reads the crossed graph as a pictorial or indicative sign for cutting across a line, then proposes that it was reused for the similar-sounding numeral. Another account documents the crossed form as 七 “seven” from oracle-bone writing onward. The original referent and proposed borrowing sequence remain uncertain.

history.text: The selected oracle-script-style image shows crossed horizontal and vertical strokes; the seal-style image shows the lower vertical stroke bending to the right. Both are modern redrawings of script forms, not photographs of artifacts. A paleographic study reports the crossed form from oracle-bone writing through early Western Han clerical forms and says the lower stroke’s rightward bend became established after the Eastern Han, possibly to distinguish 七 from 十. The account of why the bend arose is not uniform.

One proposed account says 七 was first used for a word meaning “cut,” then reused for the similar-sounding numeral; it says 刀 was added to write 切. Since other evidence records 七 for “seven” in oracle-bone writing, this proposed sequence remains disputed. No matched historical pronunciation pair for 七 and 切 is established here.
A Han-period explanation interprets the graph through the cosmological ideas of yang and yin. This is a historical interpretation, not independent evidence of what the earliest graph depicted.

uncertainties.text: The earliest graphic referent and its spoken name remain uncertain. The proposed cut interpretation and borrowing sequence are disputed, and the suggested sound connection with 切 lacks a matched reconstruction pair.

The transmitted Shijing text contains numeral uses, but the supplied evidence does not establish the date of its physical witness or the poem’s composition. It therefore does not settle the earliest surviving written attestation.

senses.period: Oracle-bone writing onward, as reported by a paleographic study
senses.text: A paleographic study reports 七 used for the numeral in oracle-bone writing and cites an oracle-bone example. This is an early attested numeral use; it does not rule out the disputed proposal of an earlier cut-related use.

senses.gloss: seven (Japanese readings なな and しち)
senses.period: Manyōshū example dated to the 8th century; later attestations also recorded
senses.text: Japanese lexical evidence records なな for “seven” in an 8th-century Manyōshū example and しち in an example from 1477. These are Japanese readings and uses, not evidence for the origin of the Chinese graph.
A specialized Japanese sense meaning “gambler” is recorded with an example dated 1744. Its development from “seven” is not explained by the evidence.

limitations.text: The evidence supports early numeral use but does not settle whether it was the graph’s original meaning. It also gives no supported semantic path from “seven” to the later Japanese sense “gambler.”

overview.text: 七 is the character for “seven.” Crossed forms are documented writing the numeral from oracle-bone writing onward. One disputed proposal says the graph first represented cutting and was later reused for the number because the words sounded alike.
